## Social Status and Mobility

### Objective and subjective social status

Research on the social foundations of distributional preferences has traditionally relied on objective indicators of social position—such as income, education, and occupational class—and on a logic of self-interest, according to which those who benefit least from redistribution tend to support it the least [@alesina_intergenerational_2018; @lindh_class_2020]. A complementary tradition focuses on subjective social status (SSS), understood as the position people believe they occupy in the social hierarchy [@adler_relationship_2000]. Both dimensions are related, but they are far from interchangeable, as the accumulated evidence shows that their correlation is only moderate [@tan_association_2020].

However, the distance between these two dimensions is not random. People assess their position by comparing themselves to their reference groups, which tends to shift their self-placement toward the center of the hierarchy, both among those at the top and those at the bottom [@evans_conditional_2022; @lindemann_contextual_2014]. In the case of Chile, one of the most unequal countries, this compression is particularly pronounced, especially among those with higher objective status [@castillo_todos_2013]. Consequently, subjective status may contain its own information, distinct from objective position, but difficult to capture based solely on its levels: using the same data from this study, what predicts participation in the 2019 protests is not subjective status itself, but rather its mismatch with objective status [@bargain_social_2026]. In other words, the more people perceive themselves as lower in the hierarchy than their objective position would suggest, the more likely they are to participate in collective action.

### Subjective social status and distributive preferences

A growing body of literature argues that the subjective dimension of status matters for distributive attitudes beyond objective resources. The central mechanism is social comparison: people evaluate the fairness of a distribution based on where they believe they stand relative to others, such that feeling lower in the hierarchy increases support for redistribution, even when actual resources remain unchanged. Experimental evidence supports this causal interpretation [@cruces_Biased_2013; @brown-iannuzzi_subjective_2015; @condon_economic_2020], and comparative survey evidence shows that subjective status predicts support for redistribution and perceived inequality independently of objective class—and even more strongly than objective class does [@duman_subjective_2019; @choi_individuals_2021; @melli_uncovering_2025; @melli_where_2025].

Two caveats qualify this picture. First, the subjective gradient depends on the context. In the most unequal countries, people with high subjective status also show greater support for redistribution, which reduces the gap between status groups [@melli_uncovering_2025; @melli_where_2025]. Highly unequal and strongly market-oriented contexts, such as Chile, could therefore be cases where subjective status contributes less than expected. Second, most of this evidence is cross-sectional and relies on differences between individuals. Panel studies suggest that redistributive preferences are quite stable, anchored in long-term economic position and early socialization, and respond only to major changes in circumstances [@ogrady_how_2019]. Even major shocks, such as job loss, produce changes that dissipate once the shock ends [@margalit_explaining_2013], although views on the justice of inequality do shift in response to individual events such as unemployment or a promotion [@hvidberg_social_2023]. Therefore, the question remains open as to whether the association between status and distributive preferences reflects stable differences between individuals or an adjustment within each individual as their status changes, which requires distinguishing between intrapersonal variation and interpersonality variation [@bell_explaining_2015].

### Past and expected mobility 

Status is not just a position, but also a trajectory: where people come from and where they hope to go can matter just as much as where they are. The literature on mobility has suggested that prospects for upward mobility can moderate demands for redistribution [@benabou_social_2001; @alesina_intergenerational_2018] and that, as with status, perceived mobility has greater attitudinal consequences than objective mobility [@gugushvili_intergenerational_2016; @hiltner_view_2024].

These effects, however, are not uniform. They vary depending on the type of policy or social service in question [@gugushvili_multilevel_2019], and when mobility is measured objectively, people tend to adopt the preferences of their destination position rather than those of their origin [@jaime-castillo_social_2019].

Expectations about the future, in particular, seem to carry more weight than past mobility [@schuck_how_2019], but the direction of their effect depends on how that upward mobility is expected to be achieved. If the next generation’s prospects are tied to public provision, optimism regarding one’s children may be accompanied by greater support for public services and less acceptance of the idea that access should depend on the ability to pay [@cojocaru_prospects_2014].

### Status, Mobility and Inequality Preferences

These debates have rarely been applied to market justice preferences—that is, to the idea that it is fair for access to services such as pensions, health care, and education to depend on the ability to pay. Comparative evidence suggests that these preferences are reinforced where private provision is most widespread [@lindh_public_2015; @immergut_it_2020], making Chile—with its widely commercialized pensions, health care, and education—a paradigmatic case. Previous studies using the same panel data have examined the role of perceived inequality [@castillo_perceptions_2025: @castillo_justification_2026], but the roles of objective and subjective status—and how they change over time—have not been addressed jointly.

The question therefore remains open as to whether market justice preferences respond to the position people occupy, the one they believe they occupy, or the one they hope to attain—and whether they do so as stable differences between individuals or as changes within each individual. Answering this requires measuring subjective status in its past, present, and future dimensions (origin, self, and children) and separating these two sources of variation.
